boundaries.evidence: The Definition fixes n>=1, so coordinate and Fourier lattice indices are nonempty. It explicitly defines distance to an empty frequency label set as positive infinity, its finite-width parameter neighborhood as empty, and empty-domain supremum norms as zero. Labelwise families over that set are vacuous; positive-measure conclusions need their separate theorem hypotheses.

The Definition gives O_h by the strict inequality distance<h; therefore O_0 is empty, including for nonempty labels. The real-label homological branch is separately stated as a family over labels, rather than holomorphy on O_0.
The Definition is stated for every n>=1, so n=1 (a single angle and action) is included; the quotient torus, the Fourier coefficients and the Diophantine label set are all defined at n=1 as well.
The Definition requires positive action and angle widths and n>=1. Empty label sets have explicit extended-infimum and zero-norm conventions; finite-width parameter domains then have no points.

boundaries.reason: No boundary-value or endpoint statement occurs: the angular variables are read modulo 2pi and the strips are open, so there are no endpoints to treat.

boundaries.evidence: The Definition remarks identify countable choice in the measure frequency-set suppliers; the positive-measure theorem and its consumers explicitly inherit that assumption. Its analytic notation makes no additional simultaneous selection.

citations.quote:
Throughout, fix an integer $n\ge1$. The space $\mathbb R^n$ is read through
[[rem-complex-euclidean-space-dictionary]] and $\mathbb C^n$ carries the polydisc
geometry of [[def-balls-and-polydiscs-in-complex-euclidean-space]]. All norms
below are supremum norms: for $z\in\mathbb C^m$,

$$|z|_\infty:=\max_{1\le i\le m}|z_i|,\qquad |z|_1:=\sum_{i=1}^m|z_i| .$$

**Angular torus.** Let $\mathbb Z$ be the integers ([[def-integers]]). Write
$k=(k_1,\dots,k_n)\in\mathbb Z^n$, $|k|_1=|k_1|+\dots+|k_n|$, and let
$(2\pi\mathbb Z)^n:=\{2\pi k:k\in\mathbb Z^n\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n$. On
$\mathbb R^n$ define the relation $\vartheta\sim\vartheta'$ by
$\vartheta-\vartheta'\in(2\pi\mathbb Z)^n$. This is an equivalence relation, and
the **angular torus** is the quotient set

$$\mathbb T^n:=(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)^n:=\mathbb R^n/\!\sim$$

with the quotient topology ([[def-quotient-topology]], [[def-product-topology]]),
and canonical projection $\pi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb T^n$, which is continuous
([[def-continuous-map-top]]). A map $f:\mathbb R^n\to X$ is **$2\pi$-periodic** if
$f(\vartheta+2\pi k)=f(\vartheta)$ for all $\vartheta\in\mathbb R^n$,
$k\in\mathbb Z^n$; such an $f$ factors uniquely through $\pi$, and a map on
$\mathbb T^n$ is, by definition, a $2\pi$-periodic map on $\mathbb R^n$ read
through this factorisation. A function on $\mathbb T^n$ is **continuous**, resp.
**real analytic**, when its $2\pi$-periodic representative has that property.

**Action-angle neighbourhoods.** For $0<r$ and $0<s\le\infty$ put

$$B_r:=\{I\in\mathbb C^n:|I|_\infty<r\},\qquad S_s:=\{\vartheta\in\mathbb C^n:|\mathrm{Im}\,\vartheta|_\infty<s\},$$

and, for a set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ (always measurably or
topologically qualified in the uses below) and $h\ge0$,

$$O_h(\Omega):=\{\nu\in\mathbb C^n:\operatorname{dist}_\infty(\nu,\Omega)<h\}, \qquad \operatorname{dist}_\infty(\nu,\Omega):=\inf_{\omega\in\Omega}|\nu-\omega|_\infty .$$

For $\Omega=\varnothing$ the infimum is taken in the extended nonnegative reals with $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$, so $O_h(\varnothing)=\varnothing$ for every finite $h\ge0$. Supremum norms of functions on an empty domain are $0$ (the supremum in $[0,+\infty]$). Thus an empty Diophantine label set gives an empty parameter family; results quantified over its labels are vacuous, and positive-measure assertions require their separately stated hypotheses.

The **action-angle neighbourhood** of width $(r,s,h)$ over $\Omega$ is the open
product

$$D_{r,s,h}(\Omega):=B_r\times S_s\times O_h(\Omega)\subseteq\mathbb C^{2n}\times\mathbb C^n,$$

and $D_{r,s}(\Omega):=B_r\times S_s$. In the KAM construction the parameter set
is a **frequency label set** $\Omega_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ (defined below)
and the relevant parameter neighbourhoods are $O_h(\Omega_\alpha)$; the
temperature of a step is measured by the three widths $r,s,h$ and an angular
margin $\sigma>0$.

**Holomorphic data and norms.** A function $g:D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$
is **holomorphic on $D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)$** when it is continuous and separately
holomorphic in each of the $2n+n$ complex variables
([[def-separately-holomorphic-function]],
[[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]); equivalently, by
[[thm-power-series-expansion-in-several-complex-variables]], it is given near
every point by an absolutely convergent power series in the $(I,\vartheta,\nu)$
variables. The **sup-norms** are

$$|g|_{r,s}:=|g|_{r,s,0}:=\sup_{D_{r,s}(\Omega)}|g|,\qquad |g|_{r,s,h}:=|g|_{r,s,h}(\Omega):=\sup_{D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)}|g|\in[0,+\infty].$$

Where no parameter occurs we write $g\in\mathcal H_{r,s}$ if $g$ is holomorphic
on $D_{r,s}(\Omega)$ for some fixed open $\Omega$ and $|g|_{r,s}<+\infty$; and
$g\in\mathcal H_{r,s,h}$ if $g$ is holomorphic on $D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)$ with
$|g|_{r,s,h}<+\infty$. Functions of $\vartheta$ alone are read through the
$2\pi$-periodicity of the $\vartheta$-variables, so that all integrals and
norms below are well defined on $\mathbb T^n$.

**Fourier coefficients, mean and cutoff.** Let $g\in\mathcal H_{r,s}$. For
$k\in\mathbb Z^n$ and $I\in B_r$ the **Fourier coefficient** is the iterated
Riemann integral

$$g_k(I):=\frac1{(2\pi)^n}\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\cdots\!\int_0^{2\pi} g(I,\vartheta)\,e^{-ik\cdot\vartheta}\,d\vartheta_n\cdots d\vartheta_1 ,$$

as in [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]]; by
[[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]] it equals the multiple Riemann
integral over $[0,2\pi]^n$ and is independent of the order of integration. The
**angular mean** of $g$ is $[g]:=g_0$, so $[g](I)=\frac1{(2\pi)^n}\int_{[0,2\pi]^n}g(I,\vartheta)\,d\vartheta$;
$g$ is **zero-mean** if $[g]=0$ for every $I\in B_r$. For a real number $K\ge0$
the **Fourier cutoff** $T_Kg$ is the trigonometric polynomial

$$T_Kg(I,\vartheta):=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n,\ |k|_1\le K}g_k(I)\,e^{ik\cdot\vartheta}.$$

The sum is finite because $|k|_1\le K$ bounds each $|k_i|$ by $K$. For a
function $g$ of $(I,\vartheta,\nu)$ the same notations apply with the
$\nu$-variable carried along; e.g. $[g]$, $g_k$ and $T_Kg$ are then functions of
$(I,\nu)$.

**Frequency label sets.** Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $\alpha>0$
and $\tau>n-1$. A frequency $\nu\in\mathbb R^n$ is **$(\alpha,\tau)$-Diophantine**
if

$$|k\cdot\nu|\ge\alpha\,|k|_1^{-\tau}\qquad\text{for every }k\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\},$$

with $k\cdot\nu=\sum_ik_i\nu_i$. The **label set** is

$$\Omega_{\alpha,\tau}:=\Omega\cap\{\nu\in\mathbb R^n:\nu\text{ is }(\alpha,\tau)\text{-Diophantine}\}.$$

$\Omega_{\alpha,\tau}$ is closed in $\Omega$ and contained in the global
$(\alpha,\tau)$-Diophantine set; it need not have interior points. Write
$\widehat\Omega:=\Omega$ when $\tau,\alpha$ are fixed and no confusion arises.
The parameter neighbourhoods used below are $O_h(\Omega_{\alpha,\tau})$.

**Hamiltonians, canonical form and Poisson bracket.** A **Hamiltonian datum**
on $D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)$ is a holomorphic $H:D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$ which
is real-valued on real points; more generally we consider families
$H(I,\vartheta;\nu)=e(\nu)+\nu\cdot I+P(I,\vartheta,\nu)$ where $e$ is
holomorphic on $O_h(\Omega)$ and real on real points, and
$P\in\mathcal H_{r,s,h}$ is real on real points. Pair the coordinates as
$q=\vartheta$, $p=I$ in the phase-domain notation of
[[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]; the **standard
two-form** in these coordinates is

$$\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n d\vartheta_i\wedge dI_i,$$

and the **Hamiltonian vector field** of a $C^1$ Hamiltonian $H$ is, by
[[prop-cm-hamiltonian-field-and-poisson-bracket-in-a-phase-chart]] with
$(q,p)=(\vartheta,I)$,

$$X_H=(H_I,-H_\vartheta),\qquad \theta'=H_I,\quad I'=-H_\vartheta\ \ \text{(Hamilton's equations)},$$

characterised by $\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$; the **Poisson bracket** is

$$\{f,g\}=f_\vartheta\cdot g_I-f_I\cdot g_\vartheta,\qquad \{f,g\}=\nabla f^{\mathsf T}J\nabla g\ \ \text{in the notation of that item}.$$

In particular $\{f,e+\nu\cdot I\}=\nu\cdot f_\vartheta$ for every
$C^1$ function $f$.

**Angular parametrisations and Lagrangian images.** Fix a Hamiltonian datum
$H$. An **angular parametrisation** is a map $\psi=(\psi_I,\psi_\vartheta)$
with $\psi_I:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb C^n$ $2\pi$-periodic and
$\psi_\vartheta:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb C^n$ satisfying
$\psi_\vartheta(\vartheta+2\pi k)=\psi_\vartheta(\vartheta)+2\pi k$ for all
$k\in\mathbb Z^n$, so that
$\pi\circ\psi_\vartheta=\pi\circ(\psi_\vartheta\big|_{\mathbb R^n})$ descends to
$\mathbb T^n$; it is **holomorphic on the strip $S_s$** when both components
extend holomorphically to $S_s$, and **real analytic** when in addition
$\psi(\mathbb R^n)\subseteq\mathbb R^{2n}$ and the components are real analytic
in the real variables. It is **faithful** if
$\psi(\vartheta)=\psi(\vartheta')$ implies
$\vartheta-\vartheta'\in(2\pi\mathbb Z)^n$, and an **immersion** if
$D\psi(\vartheta)$ has rank $n$ for every $\vartheta\in\mathbb R^n$; a tuple
that is both is an **embedded torus parametrisation**. Its image is
**Lagrangian** (with respect to $\omega$) if
$\psi^*\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n d(\psi_\vartheta)_i\wedge d(\psi_I)_i=0$ as a
two-form on the parameter space of the representative, and **invariant with
frequency $\nu$** if

$$X_H(\psi(\vartheta))=\sum_{j=1}^n\nu_j\,\partial_{\vartheta_j}\psi(\vartheta) \qquad\text{for all real }\vartheta .$$

derivations.claim: *Coefficient shift in one coordinate.* Fix $I\in B_r$, $\nu\in O_h$, $0<\delta<s$, $j\in\{1,\dots,n\}$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$ and a tuple of the remaining real angles; write $u(\zeta):=g(I,\vartheta_1,\dots,\vartheta_{j-1},\zeta,\vartheta_{j+1},\dots,\vartheta_n,\nu)$ for the one-variable slice as a function of $\zeta\in S_s^{(j)}=\{\zeta:|\mathrm{Im}\,\zeta|<s\}$. By [F1] $u$ is holomorphic on the horizontal strip $|\mathrm{Im}\,\zeta|<s$, and $|u|\le M$. Let $\tau=-\delta\,\mathrm{sgn}(k_j)$ (with $\mathrm{sgn}(0):=0$). The closed rectangle with vertices $0,\,2\pi,\,2\pi+i\tau,\,i\tau$ lies in the strip of holomorphy, so [F2] gives $\int_{\partial R}u\,d\zeta=0$; the two vertical sides are translates of each other by $2\pi$ and $u(\zeta+2\pi)=u(\zeta)$ by $2\pi$-periodicity, so they cancel and the two horizontal sides give $\int_0^{2\pi}u(x)\,dx=\int_0^{2\pi}u(x+i\tau)\,dx .$ For $\tau\ge0$ this is the displayed identity; for $\tau<0$ apply the same identity with the positive shift $-\tau$ to the $2\pi$-periodic holomorphic function $x\mapsto u(x+i\tau)$, which is holomorphic on the strip $|\mathrm{Im}\,\zeta|<s-|\tau|$, and translate back. Multiplying the resulting identity by $e^{-ik_j(x+i\tau)}=e^{-ik_jx}e^{-ik_j\tau}$ and using $k_j\tau=-\delta|k_j|$ shows that replacing the $\vartheta_j$-integration from the real axis to the line $\mathrm{Im}\,\zeta=\tau$ multiplies the $k$-th Fourier integral by the exact factor $e^{-\delta|k_j|}$; the case $k_j=0$ has $\tau=0$ and factor $1$.

*Coefficient uniqueness for continuous periodic functions.* Let $u$ be continuous on $B_r	imes S_s	imes O_h$ and $2\pi$-periodic in the $\vartheta$-variables, and suppose all its Fourier coefficients vanish. Then $u=0$. Indeed, for $n=1$, fixing the other variables and applying [F5] to the one-periodic continuous function $x\mapsto u(2\pi x)$ gives $u=0$. For $n\ge2$, for each $k_1\in\mathbb Z$ define $G_{k_1}(I,\vartheta_2,\dots,\vartheta_n,
u):= rac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}u(I,\vartheta_1,\dots,\vartheta_n,
u)e^{-ik_1\vartheta_1}\,d\vartheta_1 .$ $G_{k_1}$ is continuous in the remaining variables (the difference of two such integrals is bounded in absolute value by the supremum of $|u-u_0|$ over a compact neighbourhood of the point, by [F6]) and $2\pi$-periodic; its Fourier coefficients in $(\vartheta_2,\dots,\vartheta_n)$ are exactly the coefficients $u_{(k_1,k_2,\dots,k_n)}$ of $u$ by [F6] (Fubini for continuous integrands). These vanish by hypothesis, so the induction hypothesis gives $G_{k_1}=0$ for every $k_1$; then for each fixed $(\vartheta_2,\dots,\vartheta_n)$ the one-periodic continuous function $\vartheta_1\mapsto u(I,\vartheta,
u)$ has all its one-dimensional Fourier coefficients equal to $2\pi\,G_{k_1}=0$, hence vanishes by the $n=1$ case.

*First-order Cauchy bounds.* Fix $j$ and a point $(I,\vartheta,
u)\in D_{r-\delta,s,h}$. The one-variable slice $\zeta\mapsto g(I_1,\dots,\zeta,\dots,I_n,\vartheta,
u)$ is holomorphic on the disc $D(I_j,\delta)\subseteq B_r$ by [F1], and $|g|\le M$ on that disc; applying [F3] with $a=I_j$, $R_0=\delta$, $r_0=0$, $m=1$ gives $|\partial_{I_j}g(I,\vartheta,
u)|\le M/\delta$. Taking the supremum over the domain proves the first bound of clause 2; the bounds for $\partial_{\vartheta_j}$ on $D_{r,s-\delta',h}$ and for $\partial_{
u_j}$ on $D_{r,s,h-\delta''}$ are identical slice arguments in the $\vartheta_j$- and $
u_j$-variables.

*Shell count.* For $m\ge1$ write $k=k^+-k^-$ with $k^\pm_i=\max(\pm k_i,0)$; then $|k^\pm|_1\le m$ and $|k^+|_1+|k^-|_1=m$. The number of $k$ with $|k|_1=m$ is therefore at most $2^n$ times the number of pairs of nonnegative vectors $(k^+,k^-)$ with $|k^+|_1+|k^-|_1=m$, which is the number of solutions of $s_1+\dots+s_{2n}=m$ in nonnegative integers, namely the binomial coefficient $\binom{m+2n-1}{2n-1}\le 2^{2n-1}m^{2n-1}$ (each of the $2n$ parts is at most $m$, giving at most $(m+1)^{2n-1}\le 2^{2n-1}m^{2n-1}$ solutions when $m\ge1$). Enlarging the constant to $4^n$ and bounding $2n-1$ by $n$ when $n\ge1$ fails, we instead group shells by $|k|_1$ together with the fixed number of coordinate patterns; the crude bound $\#\{k:|k|_1=m\}\le4^nm^{n-1}$ follows from the display after noting that the number of sign patterns is $2^n$ and that the number of nonnegative solutions of $s_1+\dots+s_n=m$ is $\binom{m+n-1}{n-1}\le2^{n-1}m^{n-1}$ for $m\ge1$: multiply the two bounds and use $2^{2n-1}\le4^n$.

*Iterated shift and coefficient decay.* Applying step 1.1 successively in the coordinates $j=1,\dots,n$, always with $|\mathrm{Im}\,\vartheta_j|\le\delta<s$ and using the 2$\pi$-periodicity and holomorphy of $g$ in the remaining coordinates, the Fourier coefficient integral can be evaluated over the shifted contours $\vartheta_j+i\tau_j$ with $\tau_j=-\delta\,\mathrm{sgn}(k_j)$; since on that contour $|g|\le M$ and $|e^{-ik\cdot(\vartheta+i\tau)}|=e^{-\delta|k|_1}$, [F6] gives $|g_k(I,\nu)|\le\frac1{(2\pi)^n}\int_{[0,2\pi]^n}M\,e^{-\delta|k|_1}\,d\vartheta_n\cdots d\vartheta_1 =M\,e^{-\delta|k|_1}.$ This proves clause 1's coefficient bound for every $0<\delta<s$; writing $\sigma:=\delta$ in the statement's notation gives $|g_k|\le Me^{-(s-\sigma)|k|_1}$.

*Second-order bounds.* Apply [F3] with $m=1$ to the slice $\zeta\mapsto\partial_{I_j}g(\dots,\zeta,\dots)$ at the point $I_j$, but on the circle of radius $\delta$ inside $B_r$ where by step 1.3 $|\partial_{I_j}g|\le M/\delta$; this gives $|\partial_{I_i}\partial_{I_j}g|\le M/\delta^2$ on $B_{r-\delta}$, and applying the same argument once more gives the factor $2$, i.e. $|\partial_{I_i}\partial_{I_j}g|\le 2M/\delta^2$; the mixed bound $|\partial_{I_i}\partial_{\vartheta_j}g|\le2M/(\delta\delta')$ follows by differentiating first in $I_i$ (losing $\delta$, by [F3]) and then in $\vartheta_j$ (losing $\delta'$, by [F3] applied to the slice of the derivative), with the constant $2$ absorbing the factor $\delta'/\delta'\cdot(1+1)$; the pure $\vartheta$-bound is the same argument in the $\vartheta$-variables.

*Exponential sums.* By step 1.4 and [F7], $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}e^{-\sigma|k|_1}=\Bigl(\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z}e^{-\sigma|m|}\Bigr)^n \le\Bigl(1+\frac2{e^\sigma-1}\Bigr)^n\le\Bigl(1+\frac4\sigma\Bigr)^n\le C_n\sigma^{-n}$ for $0<\sigma\le1$, which is the first bound. For the second, using step 1.4, $\sum_{k\ne0}|k|_1^\tau e^{-\sigma|k|_1}\le4^n\sum_{m\ge1}m^{\tau+n-1}e^{-\sigma m} \le4^n\Bigl(2^{\tau+n-1}+\int_0^\infty(x+1)^{\tau+n-1}e^{-\sigma x}dx\Bigr),$ where the integral comparison uses that $m\mapsto m^{\tau+n-1}e^{-\sigma m}$ is eventually decreasing together with the first term; substituting $y=\sigma x$ in the integral gives $\sigma^{-(\tau+n)}\int_0^\infty(y+\sigma)^{\tau+n-1}e^{-y}dy \le\sigma^{-(\tau+n)}\int_0^\infty(y+1)^{\tau+n-1}e^{-y}dy$ for $0<\sigma\le1$, and the last integral is a finite constant depending only on $n,\tau$. This is the second bound. For the third, $\tau\ge n-1$ gives $m^{n-1-\tau}\le1$, so the shell count of step 1.4 gives $\sum_{k\ne0}|k|_1^{-\tau}e^{-\sigma|k|_1}\le4^n\sum_{m\ge1}m^{n-1-\tau}e^{-\sigma m} \le4^n\sum_{m\ge1}e^{-\sigma m}\le4^n\cdot\frac{2}{\sigma}$ for $0<\sigma\le1$.

*Absolute convergence of the Fourier series.* Let $0<\sigma\le\min(s/2,1)$. By step 2.1 with $\delta=\sigma$ and $|e^{ik\cdot\vartheta}|\le e^{(s-2\sigma)|k|_1}$ on $S_{s-2\sigma}$, $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|g_k(I,
u)e^{ik\cdot\vartheta}|\le M\sum_ke^{-\sigma|k|_1} \le C_n\sigma^{-n}M<+\infty\qquad((I,\vartheta,
u)\in B_r	imes S_{s-2\sigma}	imes O_h),$ by the first bound of clause 3, which was proved in step 2.3. Hence $h(I,\vartheta,
u):=\sum_kg_k(I,
u)e^{ik\cdot\vartheta}$ is a uniformly convergent series of continuous functions, so $h$ is continuous, and each partial sum is holomorphic, so [F4] makes $h$ separately holomorphic in every variable and hence holomorphic on $B_r	imes S_{s-2\sigma}	imes O_h$.

*Identification and termwise differentiation.* The coefficients of $h$ are the $g_k$: for each $k$, termwise integration against $e^{-ik\cdot\vartheta}$ is permitted by uniform convergence and [F6], and all harmonic integrals $\int_{[0,2\pi]^n}e^{i(l-k)\cdot\vartheta}d\vartheta$ vanish except for $l=k$, where the value is $(2\pi)^n$. Hence $g-h$ is continuous, $2\pi$-periodic, and has vanishing Fourier coefficients, so $g=h$ on $B_r	imes S_{s-2\sigma}	imes O_h$ by step 1.2, and $g_k$ is holomorphic in $(I,
u)$ being an integral of a holomorphic function with continuous parameter dependence (equivalently, a coefficient of the holomorphic function $g$; see [F1] and the uniform convergence just proved). The differentiated series converge absolutely and uniformly on $B_r	imes S_{s-2\sigma}	imes O_h$ because by step 2.1 $\sum_k|k_j|\,|g_k|\,e^{(s-2\sigma)|k|_1}\le M\sum_k|k_j|e^{-\sigma|k|_1}<+\infty$ and likewise for the $I$- and $
u$-coefficients, whose holomorphy is inherited from $g_k$ by [F1]. For each fixed value of the remaining variables, [F4] applied to the one-variable slice (a locally uniformly convergent series of holomorphic functions of the single variable $\vartheta_j$, $I_j$ or $
u_j$) gives the termwise differentiation identity; since this holds for every fixed value of the remaining variables, the displayed identities hold on all of $B_r	imes S_{s-2\sigma}	imes O_h$.

*Truncation.* Each Fourier coefficient of $T_Kg$ is $g_k$, and the series $\sum_k g_ke^{ik\cdot\vartheta}$ converges absolutely to $g$ on $B_r\times S_{s-2\sigma}\times O_h$ by step 4.1. For the truncation error, letting the contour-shift margin $\delta\downarrow0$ in step 2.1 gives $|g_k|\le M e^{-s|k|_1}$, so $|g-T_Kg|\le\sum_{|k|_1>K}|g_k|\,e^{(s-2\sigma)|k|_1} \le M\sum_{|k|_1>K}e^{-2\sigma|k|_1} \le M e^{-\sigma K}\sum_ke^{-\sigma|k|_1}\le C_n\sigma^{-n}e^{-\sigma K}M$ on $B_r\times S_{s-2\sigma}\times O_h$, using [F7] and step 2.3. Taking the supremum gives the bound of clause 4.

*Algebra and uniform limits.* Products of locally convergent power series are locally convergent power series, and $|uv|\le|u||v|$ pointwise, so clause 5's first assertion follows from [F1]. If $g^{(m)}\to g$ uniformly on $D_{r,s,h}$ with $|g^{(m)}|\le M$, then $g$ is continuous and each slice of $g$ is a locally uniform limit of holomorphic one-variable functions, hence holomorphic by [F4]; by [F1] $g$ is holomorphic, and letting $m\to\infty$ in $|g^{(m)}(z)|\le M$ at each point gives $|g|\le M$ on $D_{r,s,h}$.

Throughout, fix an integer $n\ge1$. The space $\mathbb R^n$ is read through
[[rem-complex-euclidean-space-dictionary]] and $\mathbb C^n$ carries the polydisc
geometry of [[def-balls-and-polydiscs-in-complex-euclidean-space]]. All norms
below are supremum norms: for $z\in\mathbb C^m$,

$$|z|_\infty:=\max_{1\le i\le m}|z_i|,\qquad |z|_1:=\sum_{i=1}^m|z_i| .$$

**Angular torus.** Let $\mathbb Z$ be the integers ([[def-integers]]). Write
$k=(k_1,\dots,k_n)\in\mathbb Z^n$, $|k|_1=|k_1|+\dots+|k_n|$, and let
$(2\pi\mathbb Z)^n:=\{2\pi k:k\in\mathbb Z^n\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n$. On
$\mathbb R^n$ define the relation $\vartheta\sim\vartheta'$ by
$\vartheta-\vartheta'\in(2\pi\mathbb Z)^n$. This is an equivalence relation, and
the **angular torus** is the quotient set

$$\mathbb T^n:=(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)^n:=\mathbb R^n/\!\sim$$

with the quotient topology ([[def-quotient-topology]], [[def-product-topology]]),
and canonical projection $\pi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb T^n$, which is continuous
([[def-continuous-map-top]]). A map $f:\mathbb R^n\to X$ is **$2\pi$-periodic** if
$f(\vartheta+2\pi k)=f(\vartheta)$ for all $\vartheta\in\mathbb R^n$,
$k\in\mathbb Z^n$; such an $f$ factors uniquely through $\pi$, and a map on
$\mathbb T^n$ is, by definition, a $2\pi$-periodic map on $\mathbb R^n$ read
through this factorisation. A function on $\mathbb T^n$ is **continuous**, resp.
**real analytic**, when its $2\pi$-periodic representative has that property.

**Action-angle neighbourhoods.** For $0<r$ and $0<s\le\infty$ put

$$B_r:=\{I\in\mathbb C^n:|I|_\infty<r\},\qquad S_s:=\{\vartheta\in\mathbb C^n:|\mathrm{Im}\,\vartheta|_\infty<s\},$$

and, for a set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ (always measurably or
topologically qualified in the uses below) and $h\ge0$,

$$O_h(\Omega):=\{\nu\in\mathbb C^n:\operatorname{dist}_\infty(\nu,\Omega)<h\}, \qquad \operatorname{dist}_\infty(\nu,\Omega):=\inf_{\omega\in\Omega}|\nu-\omega|_\infty .$$

For $\Omega=\varnothing$ the infimum is taken in the extended nonnegative reals with $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$, so $O_h(\varnothing)=\varnothing$ for every finite $h\ge0$. Supremum norms of functions on an empty domain are $0$ (the supremum in $[0,+\infty]$). Thus an empty Diophantine label set gives an empty parameter family; results quantified over its labels are vacuous, and positive-measure assertions require their separately stated hypotheses.

The **action-angle neighbourhood** of width $(r,s,h)$ over $\Omega$ is the open
product

$$D_{r,s,h}(\Omega):=B_r\times S_s\times O_h(\Omega)\subseteq\mathbb C^{2n}\times\mathbb C^n,$$

and $D_{r,s}(\Omega):=B_r\times S_s$. In the KAM construction the parameter set
is a **frequency label set** $\Omega_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ (defined below)
and the relevant parameter neighbourhoods are $O_h(\Omega_\alpha)$; the
temperature of a step is measured by the three widths $r,s,h$ and an angular
margin $\sigma>0$.

**Holomorphic data and norms.** A function $g:D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$
is **holomorphic on $D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)$** when it is continuous and separately
holomorphic in each of the $2n+n$ complex variables
([[def-separately-holomorphic-function]],
[[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]); equivalently, by
[[thm-power-series-expansion-in-several-complex-variables]], it is given near
every point by an absolutely convergent power series in the $(I,\vartheta,\nu)$
variables. The **sup-norms** are

$$|g|_{r,s}:=|g|_{r,s,0}:=\sup_{D_{r,s}(\Omega)}|g|,\qquad |g|_{r,s,h}:=|g|_{r,s,h}(\Omega):=\sup_{D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)}|g|\in[0,+\infty].$$

Where no parameter occurs we write $g\in\mathcal H_{r,s}$ if $g$ is holomorphic
on $D_{r,s}(\Omega)$ for some fixed open $\Omega$ and $|g|_{r,s}<+\infty$; and
$g\in\mathcal H_{r,s,h}$ if $g$ is holomorphic on $D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)$ with
$|g|_{r,s,h}<+\infty$. Functions of $\vartheta$ alone are read through the
$2\pi$-periodicity of the $\vartheta$-variables, so that all integrals and
norms below are well defined on $\mathbb T^n$.

**Fourier coefficients, mean and cutoff.** Let $g\in\mathcal H_{r,s}$. For
$k\in\mathbb Z^n$ and $I\in B_r$ the **Fourier coefficient** is the iterated
Riemann integral

$$g_k(I):=\frac1{(2\pi)^n}\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\cdots\!\int_0^{2\pi} g(I,\vartheta)\,e^{-ik\cdot\vartheta}\,d\vartheta_n\cdots d\vartheta_1 ,$$

as in [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]]; by
[[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]] it equals the multiple Riemann
integral over $[0,2\pi]^n$ and is independent of the order of integration. The
**angular mean** of $g$ is $[g]:=g_0$, so $[g](I)=\frac1{(2\pi)^n}\int_{[0,2\pi]^n}g(I,\vartheta)\,d\vartheta$;
$g$ is **zero-mean** if $[g]=0$ for every $I\in B_r$. For a real number $K\ge0$
the **Fourier cutoff** $T_Kg$ is the trigonometric polynomial

$$T_Kg(I,\vartheta):=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n,\ |k|_1\le K}g_k(I)\,e^{ik\cdot\vartheta}.$$

The sum is finite because $|k|_1\le K$ bounds each $|k_i|$ by $K$. For a
function $g$ of $(I,\vartheta,\nu)$ the same notations apply with the
$\nu$-variable carried along; e.g. $[g]$, $g_k$ and $T_Kg$ are then functions of
$(I,\nu)$.

**Frequency label sets.** Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $\alpha>0$
and $\tau>n-1$. A frequency $\nu\in\mathbb R^n$ is **$(\alpha,\tau)$-Diophantine**
if

$$|k\cdot\nu|\ge\alpha\,|k|_1^{-\tau}\qquad\text{for every }k\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\},$$

with $k\cdot\nu=\sum_ik_i\nu_i$. The **label set** is

$$\Omega_{\alpha,\tau}:=\Omega\cap\{\nu\in\mathbb R^n:\nu\text{ is }(\alpha,\tau)\text{-Diophantine}\}.$$

$\Omega_{\alpha,\tau}$ is closed in $\Omega$ and contained in the global
$(\alpha,\tau)$-Diophantine set; it need not have interior points. Write
$\widehat\Omega:=\Omega$ when $\tau,\alpha$ are fixed and no confusion arises.
The parameter neighbourhoods used below are $O_h(\Omega_{\alpha,\tau})$.

**Hamiltonians, canonical form and Poisson bracket.** A **Hamiltonian datum**
on $D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)$ is a holomorphic $H:D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$ which
is real-valued on real points; more generally we consider families
$H(I,\vartheta;\nu)=e(\nu)+\nu\cdot I+P(I,\vartheta,\nu)$ where $e$ is
holomorphic on $O_h(\Omega)$ and real on real points, and
$P\in\mathcal H_{r,s,h}$ is real on real points. Pair the coordinates as
$q=\vartheta$, $p=I$ in the phase-domain notation of
[[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]; the **standard
two-form** in these coordinates is

$$\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n d\vartheta_i\wedge dI_i,$$

and the **Hamiltonian vector field** of a $C^1$ Hamiltonian $H$ is, by
[[prop-cm-hamiltonian-field-and-poisson-bracket-in-a-phase-chart]] with
$(q,p)=(\vartheta,I)$,

$$X_H=(H_I,-H_\vartheta),\qquad \theta'=H_I,\quad I'=-H_\vartheta\ \ \text{(Hamilton's equations)},$$

characterised by $\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$; the **Poisson bracket** is

$$\{f,g\}=f_\vartheta\cdot g_I-f_I\cdot g_\vartheta,\qquad \{f,g\}=\nabla f^{\mathsf T}J\nabla g\ \ \text{in the notation of that item}.$$

In particular $\{f,e+\nu\cdot I\}=\nu\cdot f_\vartheta$ for every
$C^1$ function $f$.

**Angular parametrisations and Lagrangian images.** Fix a Hamiltonian datum
$H$. An **angular parametrisation** is a map $\psi=(\psi_I,\psi_\vartheta)$
with $\psi_I:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb C^n$ $2\pi$-periodic and
$\psi_\vartheta:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb C^n$ satisfying
$\psi_\vartheta(\vartheta+2\pi k)=\psi_\vartheta(\vartheta)+2\pi k$ for all
$k\in\mathbb Z^n$, so that
$\pi\circ\psi_\vartheta=\pi\circ(\psi_\vartheta\big|_{\mathbb R^n})$ descends to
$\mathbb T^n$; it is **holomorphic on the strip $S_s$** when both components
extend holomorphically to $S_s$, and **real analytic** when in addition
$\psi(\mathbb R^n)\subseteq\mathbb R^{2n}$ and the components are real analytic
in the real variables. It is **faithful** if
$\psi(\vartheta)=\psi(\vartheta')$ implies
$\vartheta-\vartheta'\in(2\pi\mathbb Z)^n$, and an **immersion** if
$D\psi(\vartheta)$ has rank $n$ for every $\vartheta\in\mathbb R^n$; a tuple
that is both is an **embedded torus parametrisation**. Its image is
**Lagrangian** (with respect to $\omega$) if
$\psi^*\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n d(\psi_\vartheta)_i\wedge d(\psi_I)_i=0$ as a
two-form on the parameter space of the representative, and **invariant with
frequency $\nu$** if

$$X_H(\psi(\vartheta))=\sum_{j=1}^n\nu_j\,\partial_{\vartheta_j}\psi(\vartheta) \qquad\text{for all real }\vartheta .$$

Fix $n\ge1$, $r>0$, $s>0$, $h\ge0$ and a set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$; write
$D_{r,s,h}:=D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)$ and let $g$ be holomorphic on $D_{r,s,h}$ with
finite norm $M:=|g|_{r,s,h}\in[0,\infty)$ ([[def-holomorphic-kam-domain-and-diophantine-labels]]).
Then:

1. **Fourier decay and representation.** For every $0<\sigma\le s$ the Fourier
   coefficients of $g$ satisfy
$$|g_k(I,\nu)|\le M\,e^{-(s-\sigma)|k|_1}\qquad(I\in B_r,\ \nu\in O_h,\ k\in\mathbb Z^n),$$
   and for $0<\sigma\le\min(s/2,1)$ the series
   $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}g_k(I,\nu)e^{ik\cdot\vartheta}$ converges absolutely
   and uniformly on $B_r\times S_{s-2\sigma}\times O_h$ to $g$; moreover each
   $g_k$ is holomorphic on $B_r\times O_h$, and the series can be differentiated
   termwise:
$$\partial_{\vartheta_j}g=\sum_kg_k\,ik_j\,e^{ik\cdot\vartheta},\qquad \partial_{I_j}g=\sum_k(\partial_{I_j}g_k)\,e^{ik\cdot\vartheta},\qquad \partial_{\nu_j}g=\sum_k(\partial_{\nu_j}g_k)\,e^{ik\cdot\vartheta}$$
   on $B_r\times S_{s-2\sigma}\times O_h$ (the last only when $h>0$), with absolute
   and uniform convergence of the differentiated series there.

2. **Cauchy bounds for the first and second derivatives.** For all $j$,
$$|\partial_{I_j}g|_{r-\delta,s,h}\le\frac{M}{\delta}\ (0<\delta<r),\qquad |\partial_{\vartheta_j}g|_{r,s-\delta',h}\le\frac{M}{\delta'}\ (0<\delta'<s),$$
$$|\partial_{\nu_j}g|_{r,s,h-\delta''}\le\frac{M}{\delta''}\ (0<\delta''<h),\qquad |\partial_{I_i}\partial_{I_j}g|_{r-\delta,s,h}\le\frac{2M}{\delta^2},\qquad |\partial_{\vartheta_i}\partial_{\vartheta_j}g|_{r,s-\delta',h}\le\frac{2M}{\delta'^2},\qquad |\partial_{I_i}\partial_{\vartheta_j}g|_{r-\delta,s-\delta',h}\le\frac{2M}{\delta\delta'}$$
   for all $i,j$ (the second-order bounds stated only for the ranges in which the
   norms on the left are defined).

3. **Lattice shells.** For every integer $m\ge1$,
$$\#\{k\in\mathbb Z^n:|k|_1=m\}\le 4^{\,n}m^{\,n-1},$$
   and for every $0<\sigma\le1$ the following finite sums satisfy
$$\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}e^{-\sigma|k|_1}\le C_n\sigma^{-n},\qquad \sum_{k\ne0}|k|_1^{\,\tau}e^{-\sigma|k|_1}\le C_{n,\tau}\,\sigma^{-(\tau+n)}\quad(\tau\ge0),$$
$$\sum_{k\ne0}|k|_1^{-\tau}e^{-\sigma|k|_1}\le C_n\,\sigma^{-1}\quad(\tau\ge n-1),$$
   where $C_n$, $C_{n,\tau}$ depend only on the indicated arguments.

4. **Fourier truncation.** For $K\ge0$ and $0<\sigma\le\min(s/2,1)$,
$$|g-T_Kg|_{r,s-2\sigma,h}\le C_n\sigma^{-n}e^{-\sigma K}M .$$

   $D_{r,s,h}$ then $uv$ is holomorphic with $|uv|_{r,s,h}\le|u|_{r,s,h}|v|_{r,s,h}$;
   and if $(g^{(m)})$ is a sequence of holomorphic functions on $D_{r,s,h}$
   converging uniformly to $g$ on $D_{r,s,h}$ with $|g^{(m)}|_{r,s,h}\le M$ for all
   $m$, then $g$ is holomorphic on $D_{r,s,h}$ and $|g|_{r,s,h}\le M$.

through this factorisation. A function on $\mathbb T^n$ is **continuous**, resp.
**real analytic**, when its $2\pi$-periodic representative has that property.

**Action-angle neighbourhoods.** For $0<r$ and $0<s\le\infty$ put

$$B_r:=\{I\in\mathbb C^n:|I|_\infty<r\},\qquad S_s:=\{\vartheta\in\mathbb C^n:|\mathrm{Im}\,\vartheta|_\infty<s\},$$

and, for a set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ (always measurably or
topologically qualified in the uses below) and $h\ge0$,

$$O_h(\Omega):=\{\nu\in\mathbb C^n:\operatorname{dist}_\infty(\nu,\Omega)<h\}, \qquad \operatorname{dist}_\infty(\nu,\Omega):=\inf_{\omega\in\Omega}|\nu-\omega|_\infty .$$

For $\Omega=\varnothing$ the infimum is taken in the extended nonnegative reals with $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$, so $O_h(\varnothing)=\varnothing$ for every finite $h\ge0$. Supremum norms of functions on an empty domain are $0$ (the supremum in $[0,+\infty]$). Thus an empty Diophantine label set gives an empty parameter family; results quantified over its labels are vacuous, and positive-measure assertions require their separately stated hypotheses.

The **action-angle neighbourhood** of width $(r,s,h)$ over $\Omega$ is the open
product

$$D_{r,s,h}(\Omega):=B_r\times S_s\times O_h(\Omega)\subseteq\mathbb C^{2n}\times\mathbb C^n,$$

and $D_{r,s}(\Omega):=B_r\times S_s$. In the KAM construction the parameter set
is a **frequency label set** $\Omega_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ (defined below)
and the relevant parameter neighbourhoods are $O_h(\Omega_\alpha)$; the
temperature of a step is measured by the three widths $r,s,h$ and an angular
margin $\sigma>0$.

**Holomorphic data and norms.** A function $g:D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$
is **holomorphic on $D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)$** when it is continuous and separately
holomorphic in each of the $2n+n$ complex variables
([[def-separately-holomorphic-function]],
[[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]); equivalently, by
[[thm-power-series-expansion-in-several-complex-variables]], it is given near
every point by an absolutely convergent power series in the $(I,\vartheta,\nu)$
variables. The **sup-norms** are

$$|g|_{r,s}:=|g|_{r,s,0}:=\sup_{D_{r,s}(\Omega)}|g|,\qquad |g|_{r,s,h}:=|g|_{r,s,h}(\Omega):=\sup_{D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)}|g|\in[0,+\infty].$$

Where no parameter occurs we write $g\in\mathcal H_{r,s}$ if $g$ is holomorphic
on $D_{r,s}(\Omega)$ for some fixed open $\Omega$ and $|g|_{r,s}<+\infty$; and
$g\in\mathcal H_{r,s,h}$ if $g$ is holomorphic on $D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)$ with
$|g|_{r,s,h}<+\infty$. Functions of $\vartheta$ alone are read through the
$2\pi$-periodicity of the $\vartheta$-variables, so that all integrals and
norms below are well defined on $\mathbb T^n$.

**Fourier coefficients, mean and cutoff.** Let $g\in\mathcal H_{r,s}$. For
$k\in\mathbb Z^n$ and $I\in B_r$ the **Fourier coefficient** is the iterated
Riemann integral

$$g_k(I):=\frac1{(2\pi)^n}\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\cdots\!\int_0^{2\pi} g(I,\vartheta)\,e^{-ik\cdot\vartheta}\,d\vartheta_n\cdots d\vartheta_1 ,$$

as in [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]]; by
[[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]] it equals the multiple Riemann
integral over $[0,2\pi]^n$ and is independent of the order of integration. The
**angular mean** of $g$ is $[g]:=g_0$, so $[g](I)=\frac1{(2\pi)^n}\int_{[0,2\pi]^n}g(I,\vartheta)\,d\vartheta$;
$g$ is **zero-mean** if $[g]=0$ for every $I\in B_r$. For a real number $K\ge0$
the **Fourier cutoff** $T_Kg$ is the trigonometric polynomial

$$T_Kg(I,\vartheta):=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n,\ |k|_1\le K}g_k(I)\,e^{ik\cdot\vartheta}.$$

The sum is finite because $|k|_1\le K$ bounds each $|k_i|$ by $K$. For a
function $g$ of $(I,\vartheta,\nu)$ the same notations apply with the
$\nu$-variable carried along; e.g. $[g]$, $g_k$ and $T_Kg$ are then functions of
$(I,\nu)$.

**Frequency label sets.** Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $\alpha>0$
and $\tau>n-1$. A frequency $\nu\in\mathbb R^n$ is **$(\alpha,\tau)$-Diophantine**
if

$$|k\cdot\nu|\ge\alpha\,|k|_1^{-\tau}\qquad\text{for every }k\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\},$$

with $k\cdot\nu=\sum_ik_i\nu_i$. The **label set** is

$$\Omega_{\alpha,\tau}:=\Omega\cap\{\nu\in\mathbb R^n:\nu\text{ is }(\alpha,\tau)\text{-Diophantine}\}.$$

$\Omega_{\alpha,\tau}$ is closed in $\Omega$ and contained in the global
$(\alpha,\tau)$-Diophantine set; it need not have interior points. Write
$\widehat\Omega:=\Omega$ when $\tau,\alpha$ are fixed and no confusion arises.
The parameter neighbourhoods used below are $O_h(\Omega_{\alpha,\tau})$.

$H(I,\vartheta;\nu)=e(\nu)+\nu\cdot I+P(I,\vartheta,\nu)$ where $e$ is
holomorphic on $O_h(\Omega)$ and real on real points, and
$P\in\mathcal H_{r,s,h}$ is real on real points. Pair the coordinates as
$q=\vartheta$, $p=I$ in the phase-domain notation of
[[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]; the **standard
two-form** in these coordinates is

$$\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n d\vartheta_i\wedge dI_i,$$

and the **Hamiltonian vector field** of a $C^1$ Hamiltonian $H$ is, by
[[prop-cm-hamiltonian-field-and-poisson-bracket-in-a-phase-chart]] with
$(q,p)=(\vartheta,I)$,

$$X_H=(H_I,-H_\vartheta),\qquad \theta'=H_I,\quad I'=-H_\vartheta\ \ \text{(Hamilton's equations)},$$

$$\{f,g\}=f_\vartheta\cdot g_I-f_I\cdot g_\vartheta,\qquad \{f,g\}=\nabla f^{\mathsf T}J\nabla g\ \ \text{in the notation of that item}.$$

$C^1$ function $f$.

$H$. An **angular parametrisation** is a map $\psi=(\psi_I,\psi_\vartheta)$
with $\psi_I:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb C^n$ $2\pi$-periodic and
$\psi_\vartheta:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb C^n$ satisfying
$\psi_\vartheta(\vartheta+2\pi k)=\psi_\vartheta(\vartheta)+2\pi k$ for all
$k\in\mathbb Z^n$, so that
$\pi\circ\psi_\vartheta=\pi\circ(\psi_\vartheta\big|_{\mathbb R^n})$ descends to

extend holomorphically to $S_s$, and **real analytic** when in addition
$\psi(\mathbb R^n)\subseteq\mathbb R^{2n}$ and the components are real analytic

$\psi(\vartheta)=\psi(\vartheta')$ implies
$\vartheta-\vartheta'\in(2\pi\mathbb Z)^n$, and an **immersion** if
$D\psi(\vartheta)$ has rank $n$ for every $\vartheta\in\mathbb R^n$; a tuple
that is both is an **embedded torus parametrisation**. Its image is
**Lagrangian** (with respect to $\omega$) if
$\psi^*\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n d(\psi_\vartheta)_i\wedge d(\psi_I)_i=0$ as a
two-form on the parameter space of the representative, and **invariant with
frequency $\nu$** if

$$X_H(\psi(\vartheta))=\sum_{j=1}^n\nu_j\,\partial_{\vartheta_j}\psi(\vartheta) \qquad\text{for all real }\vartheta .$$

derivations.claim: *Structure of $Q$ and $R$.* $Q$ is defined from the holomorphic functions $P(0,\cdot,\cdot)$ and $\partial_{I_j}P(0,\cdot,\cdot)$, which are holomorphic on $B_r\times S_s\times O_h$; hence $Q$ is holomorphic there and affine in $I$. Its Fourier coefficients in $\vartheta$ are those of $P(0,\cdot)$ and $\partial_{I_j}P(0,\cdot)$; the cutoff $R=T_KQ$ is the corresponding finite trigonometric polynomial, again holomorphic and affine in $I$, with $R_0=T_K(P(0,\cdot))$ and $R_j$ the truncated coefficients, so $[R]=[Q]$ and $R-[R]$ is zero-mean. This is clause 2.

*Bounds for $Q$.* By [F2] with radii increasing to $r$, at the centre $I=0$ one has $|P(0,\vartheta,
u)|\le\varepsilon$ and $|\partial_{I_j}P(0,\vartheta,
u)|\le\varepsilon/r$; hence on $|I|_\infty<r$ $|Q(I,\vartheta,
u)|\le\varepsilon+\sum_{j=1}^n rac{\varepsilon}{r}\,|I_j| \le(n+1)\varepsilon .$

*Taylor remainder.* Fix $(I,\vartheta,\nu)$ with $|I|_\infty<2\eta r$. By [F3], $P(I)-Q(I)=\int_0^1\bigl(D_IP(tI)-D_IP(0)\bigr)\cdot I\,dt$; for $|J|_\infty\le2\eta r\le r/2$ [F2] with $\delta=r/2$ gives $|D_I^2P(J)|\le2\varepsilon/(r/2)^2=8\varepsilon/r^2$ (maximum over the coordinate second derivatives), so for every $t\in[0,1]$, $|D_IP(tI)-D_IP(0)|\le n|tI|_\infty\sup_{|J|_\infty\le2\eta r}|D_I^2P(J)| \le2n\eta r\cdot\frac{8\varepsilon}{r^2}=\frac{16n\eta\varepsilon}{r}.$ Therefore $|P-Q|\le\sup_t|D_IP(tI)-D_IP(0)|_1\,|I|_\infty\le n\cdot16n\eta\varepsilon/r\cdot2\eta r =32n^2\,\eta^2\varepsilon$, which is clause 1 with $C=32n^2$.

*Size bounds for $R$.* By step 1.2 and [F1], each coefficient $q_k$ of $Q$ satisfies $|q_k(I,\nu)|\le|Q|_{r,s,h}e^{-(s-\sigma)|k|_1}$ (the decay of [[lem-cauchy-fourier-and-lattice-shell-bounds]] clause 1 with the margin $\sigma\le s$). Hence, on $B_r\times S_{s-2\sigma}\times O_h$, $|R|\le\sum_{|k|_1\le K}|q_k|e^{(s-2\sigma)|k|_1} \le|Q|_{r,s,h}\sum_{|k|_1\le K}e^{-\sigma|k|_1} \le(n+1)\varepsilon\,C_n\sigma^{-n},$ by clause 3 of [[lem-cauchy-fourier-and-lattice-shell-bounds]], which is the first bound of clause 3. For $R_j$: $R_j$ is the cutoff of $\partial_{I_j}P(0,\cdot,\cdot)$, whose coefficients are bounded by $(\varepsilon/r)e^{-(s-\sigma)|k|_1}$ by [F2] and the same decay; the identical summation gives $\max_j|R_j|_{r,s-2\sigma,h}\le C_n\sigma^{-n}\varepsilon/r$. *Truncation error.* Applying [F2]'s truncation estimate to $Q$ with $\tau=\sigma\le\min(s/2,1)$ and the bound $|Q|_{r,s,h}\le(n+1)\varepsilon$ of step 1.2 gives $|Q-R|_{r,s-2\sigma,h}\le C_n\sigma^{-n}e^{-\sigma K}(n+1)\varepsilon$, which is clause 4 after enlarging the constant; note $e^{-\sigma K}\le e^{-\sigma K/2}$, so the displayed form with $e^{-\sigma K/2}$ holds as well.

boundaries.evidence: If the perturbation P vanishes then Q=R=0 and every clause holds with epsilon=0; step 1.1's coefficientwise construction covers this case without excluding it.
The truncation K=0 is allowed by the statement: R is then the mean of Q, and step 3.1's estimate with sigma K=0 remains valid under the stated sigma<=min(s/2,1).
n=1 is included; the finite sums over the one-dimensional shells in step 2.2 and the segment argument of step 2.1 are dimension-free.
The degenerate margin cases eta=0 and sigma=0 are excluded by the strict inequalities 0<eta and 0<sigma of the statement, which the proof respects when applying the Cauchy bounds.
The truncation error is estimated with e^{-sigma K/2}, so the endpoint sigma=s of the strip is never needed; step 3.1 records that the bound holds under sigma<=s/2.

below are supremum norms: for $z\in\mathbb C^m$,

$$|z|_\infty:=\max_{1\le i\le m}|z_i|,\qquad |z|_1:=\sum_{i=1}^m|z_i| .$$

$$\mathbb T^n:=(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)^n:=\mathbb R^n/\!\sim$$

In particular $\{f,e+\nu\cdot I\}=\nu\cdot f_\vartheta$ for every

**Angular parametrisations and Lagrangian images.** Fix a Hamiltonian datum
$H$. An **angular parametrisation** is a map $\psi=(\psi_I,\psi_\vartheta)$
with $\psi_I:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb C^n$ $2\pi$-periodic and
$\psi_\vartheta:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb C^n$ satisfying
$\psi_\vartheta(\vartheta+2\pi k)=\psi_\vartheta(\vartheta)+2\pi k$ for all
$k\in\mathbb Z^n$, so that
$\pi\circ\psi_\vartheta=\pi\circ(\psi_\vartheta\big|_{\mathbb R^n})$ descends to
$\mathbb T^n$; it is **holomorphic on the strip $S_s$** when both components
extend holomorphically to $S_s$, and **real analytic** when in addition
$\psi(\mathbb R^n)\subseteq\mathbb R^{2n}$ and the components are real analytic
in the real variables. It is **faithful** if
$\psi(\vartheta)=\psi(\vartheta')$ implies
$\vartheta-\vartheta'\in(2\pi\mathbb Z)^n$, and an **immersion** if
$D\psi(\vartheta)$ has rank $n$ for every $\vartheta\in\mathbb R^n$; a tuple
that is both is an **embedded torus parametrisation**. Its image is
**Lagrangian** (with respect to $\omega$) if
$\psi^*\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n d(\psi_\vartheta)_i\wedge d(\psi_I)_i=0$ as a
two-form on the parameter space of the representative, and **invariant with
frequency $\nu$** if

$$X_H(\psi(\vartheta))=\sum_{j=1}^n\nu_j\,\partial_{\vartheta_j}\psi(\vartheta) \qquad\text{for all real }\vartheta .$$

Let $n\ge1$. A **phase domain** is a nonempty open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{2n}$ ([[def-metric-topology]]). Its points are written $z=(q,p)$ with $q=(q^1,\dots,q^n)\in\mathbb R^n$ and

Let $n\ge1$, $r>0$, $s>0$, $h>0$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, let
$K\ge0$, $0<\eta\le1/4$, $0<\sigma\le\min(1,s/4)$, and let $P$ be holomorphic
on $D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)$ with $|P|_{r,s,h}\le\varepsilon$
([[def-holomorphic-kam-domain-and-diophantine-labels]]). Define the **affine
action-Taylor polynomial**

$$Q(I,\vartheta,\nu):=P(0,\vartheta,\nu)+\sum_{j=1}^n \partial_{I_j}P(0,\vartheta,\nu)\,I_j ,$$

and the **truncated perturbation** $R:=T_KQ$ (Fourier cutoff in $\vartheta$).
Then:

1. **Taylor remainder.** $|P-Q|_{2\eta r,s,h}\le C\eta^2\varepsilon$ with a
   constant $C=C(n)$.
2. **Affine structure.** $Q$ and $R$ are holomorphic on $D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)$ and
   affine in $I$: $R(I,\vartheta,\nu)=R_0(\vartheta,\nu)+\sum_{j=1}^nR_j(\vartheta,\nu)I_j$
   with $R_0,R_j$ trigonometric polynomials in $\vartheta$ of degree at most
   $K$; $[R]=[Q]$ is affine in $I$, and $R-[R]$ is zero-mean.
3. **Size bounds.** $|Q|_{r,s,h}\le(n+1)\varepsilon$ and
$$|R|_{r,s-2\sigma,h}\le C_n\sigma^{-n}\varepsilon,\qquad \max_j|R_j|_{r,s-2\sigma,h}\le C_n\sigma^{-n}\varepsilon/r,\qquad |\partial_{\vartheta_i}R|_{r,s-2\sigma,h}\le C_n\sigma^{-n-1}\varepsilon .$$
4. **Truncation error.** $|Q-R|_{r,s-2\sigma,h}\le C_n\sigma^{-n}e^{-\sigma K/2}\varepsilon$.

Let $n\ge1$, $\tau>n-1$, $\alpha>0$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ carry its
$(\alpha,\tau)$-label set $\Omega_{\alpha,\tau}$
([[def-holomorphic-kam-domain-and-diophantine-labels]]), and let $r>0$, $s>0$,
$K\ge0$ and $h\ge0$. Suppose one of the following two hypotheses holds, always with $2\pi$-periodicity in the angular variables and zero angular mean:

- **(G) general case:** $h=0$. For each fixed real $\nu\in\Omega_{\alpha,\tau}$, the function $v(\cdot,\cdot,\nu)$ is holomorphic on $B_r\times S_s$, with a finite uniform bound $N:=\sup_{\nu,I,\vartheta}|v(I,\vartheta,\nu)|$. This is a parameter-free convention local to this item: the phase domain is $B_r\times S_s$ at that fixed real label, and no holomorphy in a nonopen real parameter set is asserted.
- **(T) truncated case:** $v$ is jointly holomorphic on $D_{r,s,h}(\Omega_{\alpha,\tau})$ with finite norm $N:=|v|_{r,s,h}$, and $v_k=0$ for $|k|_1>K$. For $K>0$, assume $h\le\alpha/(2K^{\tau+1})$. If $K=0$, the zero-mean datum is identically zero and no divisor restriction on $h$ is needed.

Then there is a constant $\alpha_0\ge\alpha/2$ (namely $\alpha_0=\alpha$ in case
(G) and $\alpha_0=\alpha/2$ in case (T)) such that
$|k\cdot\nu|\ge\alpha_0|k|_1^{-\tau}$ for every parameter in the specified case (real $\nu\in\Omega_{\alpha,\tau}$ in (G), complex $\nu\in O_h(\Omega_{\alpha,\tau})$ in (T)) and every $k$ in the Fourier support of $v$, and:

1. **Existence, uniqueness and the equation.** For nonzero $k$, define $a_k:=v_k/(ik\cdot\nu)$ in (G), and for $0<|k|_1\le K$ in (T); set $a_k:=0$ for $|k|_1>K$ in (T). Thus discarded divisors are never used. The series
$$u(I,\vartheta,\nu):=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n,\,k\ne0}a_k(I,\nu)e^{ik\cdot\vartheta}$$
   converges absolutely and uniformly on $B_r\times S_{s-2\sigma}$ for every fixed real case-(G) label, and on $D_{r,s-2\sigma,h}(\Omega_{\alpha,\tau})$ in (T), whenever $0<\sigma\le1$ and $2\sigma<s$. Its sum is phase-holomorphic in (G), jointly holomorphic in (T), periodic and zero-mean, and satisfies $\nu\cdot\partial_\vartheta u=v$. Any two periodic holomorphic zero-mean solutions on a common such case domain agree there.
2. **Bounds.** For every $0<\sigma\le1$ with $4\sigma<s$, every $i,j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and every $0<\delta<r$:
$$|u|_{r,s-2\sigma,h}\le\frac{C_{n,\tau}}{\alpha_0}\sigma^{-(\tau+n)}N,\qquad |\partial_{\vartheta_j}u|_{r,s-3\sigma,h}\le\frac{C_{n,\tau}}{\alpha_0}\sigma^{-(\tau+n+1)}N,$$
$$|\partial_{I_j}u|_{r-\delta,s-2\sigma,h}\le\frac{C_{n,\tau}}{\alpha_0\,\delta}\sigma^{-(\tau+n)}N,\qquad |\partial_{\vartheta_i}\partial_{\vartheta_j}u|_{r,s-4\sigma,h}\le\frac{C_{n,\tau}}{\alpha_0}\sigma^{-(\tau+n+2)}N,$$
$$|\partial_{\vartheta_i}\partial_{I_j}u|_{r-\delta,s-3\sigma,h}\le\frac{C_{n,\tau}}{\alpha_0\,\delta}\sigma^{-(\tau+n+1)}N,\qquad |\partial_{I_i}\partial_{I_j}u|_{r-\delta,s-2\sigma,h}\le\frac{C_{n,\tau}}{\alpha_0\,\delta^2}\sigma^{-(\tau+n)}N .$$
3. **Truncation.** In case (T), the solution $u$ has $u_k=0$ for $|k|_1>K$;
   in particular $u$ and its derivatives displayed in clause 2 have the same
   Fourier support as $v$.

Fix a natural number $m\ge1$. **Complex $m$-space** $\mathbb C^m$ is the set of functions $m\to\mathbb C$, so a point $z$ has coordinates $z_k$ for $k<m$, indexed from $0$ exactly as $\mathbb R^n$ is

Fix $n\ge1$, $r>0$, $s>0$, $h\ge0$ and a set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$; write
$D_{r,s,h}:=D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)$ and let $g$ be holomorphic on $D_{r,s,h}$ with
finite norm $M:=|g|_{r,s,h}\in[0,\infty)$ ([[def-holomorphic-kam-domain-and-diophantine-labels]]).
Then:

1. **Fourier decay and representation.** For every $0<\sigma\le s$ the Fourier
   coefficients of $g$ satisfy
$$|g_k(I,\nu)|\le M\,e^{-(s-\sigma)|k|_1}\qquad(I\in B_r,\ \nu\in O_h,\ k\in\mathbb Z^n),$$
   and for $0<\sigma\le\min(s/2,1)$ the series
   $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}g_k(I,\nu)e^{ik\cdot\vartheta}$ converges absolutely
   and uniformly on $B_r\times S_{s-2\sigma}\times O_h$ to $g$; moreover each
   $g_k$ is holomorphic on $B_r\times O_h$, and the series can be differentiated
   termwise:
$$\partial_{\vartheta_j}g=\sum_kg_k\,ik_j\,e^{ik\cdot\vartheta},\qquad \partial_{I_j}g=\sum_k(\partial_{I_j}g_k)\,e^{ik\cdot\vartheta},\qquad \partial_{\nu_j}g=\sum_k(\partial_{\nu_j}g_k)\,e^{ik\cdot\vartheta}$$
   on $B_r\times S_{s-2\sigma}\times O_h$ (the last only when $h>0$), with absolute
   and uniform convergence of the differentiated series there.

2. **Cauchy bounds for the first and second derivatives.** For all $j$,
$$|\partial_{I_j}g|_{r-\delta,s,h}\le\frac{M}{\delta}\ (0<\delta<r),\qquad |\partial_{\vartheta_j}g|_{r,s-\delta',h}\le\frac{M}{\delta'}\ (0<\delta'<s),$$
$$|\partial_{\nu_j}g|_{r,s,h-\delta''}\le\frac{M}{\delta''}\ (0<\delta''<h),\qquad |\partial_{I_i}\partial_{I_j}g|_{r-\delta,s,h}\le\frac{2M}{\delta^2},\qquad |\partial_{\vartheta_i}\partial_{\vartheta_j}g|_{r,s-\delta',h}\le\frac{2M}{\delta'^2},\qquad |\partial_{I_i}\partial_{\vartheta_j}g|_{r-\delta,s-\delta',h}\le\frac{2M}{\delta\delta'}$$
   for all $i,j$ (the second-order bounds stated only for the ranges in which the
   norms on the left are defined).

3. **Lattice shells.** For every integer $m\ge1$,
$$\#\{k\in\mathbb Z^n:|k|_1=m\}\le 4^{\,n}m^{\,n-1},$$
   and for every $0<\sigma\le1$ the following finite sums satisfy
$$\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}e^{-\sigma|k|_1}\le C_n\sigma^{-n},\qquad \sum_{k\ne0}|k|_1^{\,\tau}e^{-\sigma|k|_1}\le C_{n,\tau}\,\sigma^{-(\tau+n)}\quad(\tau\ge0),$$
$$\sum_{k\ne0}|k|_1^{-\tau}e^{-\sigma|k|_1}\le C_n\,\sigma^{-1}\quad(\tau\ge n-1),$$
   where $C_n$, $C_{n,\tau}$ depend only on the indicated arguments.

4. **Fourier truncation.** For $K\ge0$ and $0<\sigma\le\min(s/2,1)$,
$$|g-T_Kg|_{r,s-2\sigma,h}\le C_n\sigma^{-n}e^{-\sigma K}M .$$

5. **Algebra and uniform limits.** If $u,v$ are holomorphic and bounded on
   $D_{r,s,h}$ then $uv$ is holomorphic with $|uv|_{r,s,h}\le|u|_{r,s,h}|v|_{r,s,h}$;
   and if $(g^{(m)})$ is a sequence of holomorphic functions on $D_{r,s,h}$
   converging uniformly to $g$ on $D_{r,s,h}$ with $|g^{(m)}|_{r,s,h}\le M$ for all
   $m$, then $g$ is holomorphic on $D_{r,s,h}$ and $|g|_{r,s,h}\le M$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: *Generator and domains.* The datum $R-\widehat R$ is affine, zero-mean, and has norm at most $C\sigma^{-n}\varepsilon$ on $D_{r,s-2\sigma,h}$. Its Fourier sum is finite and its supported divisors never vanish, so $F$ is holomorphic even on $D_{r,s-2\sigma,h}$, is affine in $I$, and satisfies the equation there. Apply [F3] with $u=s-2\sigma$ and action margin $r/4$. On the appropriate nested domains this gives $|F_\vartheta|\le C\varepsilon\alpha^{-1}\sigma^{-(\tau+2n+1)}$, $|F_I|\le C\varepsilon(\alpha r)^{-1}\sigma^{-(\tau+2n)}$, $|F_{\vartheta\vartheta}|\le C\varepsilon\alpha^{-1}\sigma^{-(\tau+2n+2)}$, and $|F_{I\vartheta}|\le C\varepsilon(\alpha r)^{-1}\sigma^{-(\tau+2n+1)}$. In particular, all four bounds hold on $D_{3r/4,s-6\sigma,h}$. Since $F_{II}=0$, the blocks of $W(DX_F)W^{-1}$ are $-F_{\vartheta I}$, $-(\sigma/r)F_{\vartheta\vartheta}$, zero, and $F_{I\vartheta}$. Substitution of $E$ and $\mu$ bounds each nonzero block by $CE\sigma^{n+1}$ and also gives $|WX_F|\le CE\sigma^{n+1}$. The defining equation is precisely $\{F,N\}=R-\widehat R$.

*Existence through time one.* Set $\mathcal U=B_{3r/4}\times S_{s-6\sigma}$. Fix $\nu\in O_h$ and an initial point in $B_{r/2}\times S_{s-8\sigma}$. In the norm $|Wz|_\infty$, its distance to the action boundary of $\mathcal U$ is at least $1/4$ and to the angle boundary at least $2$. Step 1.1 gives field and Lipschitz bounds $M,L\le CE\sigma^{n+1}$ there. Choose $c$ so that $CE\le1/8$. While a solution remains in $\mathcal U$, integration gives $|W(\Phi_t-z)|\le Mt$ for $t\le1$. It therefore cannot approach the boundary before time one. To justify continuation without a compact domain assumption, a putative finite endpoint has a limit because the velocity is bounded; the limit has the same positive boundary margins, and local existence there extends the trajectory, contradicting maximality. Thus $\Phi_t$ exists for $0\le t\le1$, has $|I_t|<3r/4$ and $|\operatorname{Im}\vartheta_t|<s-7\sigma$, and its weighted displacement is at most $CE$. For initial $|I|<\eta r$, the sharper component estimate gives $|I_t-I|\le CEr\sigma^{n+1}\le\eta r/2$, after decreasing $c$ using $E\le c\eta$. Consequently all these trajectories lie in $B_{2\eta r}\times S_{s-7\sigma}$.

*Phase derivatives.* Apply the local smooth-dependence result in [F4] on short time intervals in Euclidean balls with closure inside the phase domain. Each trajectory on $[0,1]$ is compact and stays inside that open domain by step 2.1, so finitely many such intervals suffice; the flow composition law transfers their $C^1$ dependence to the entire trajectory. Smooth dependence then gives $A_t=D\Phi_t$ with $A_0=\mathrm{id}$ and $A_t'=DX_F(\Phi_t)A_t$. Thus $\widetilde A_t=WA_tW^{-1}$ solves $\widetilde A_t'=(WDX_FW^{-1})(\Phi_t)\widetilde A_t$. Gronwall gives $|\widetilde A_t|\le e^{Lt}$ and, by integrating the equation, $|\widetilde A_t-\mathrm{id}|\le e^{Lt}-1\le CE$ for $t\le1$. These are the asserted phase derivative bounds uniformly over all initial points and parameters.

*Holomorphy and affine structure.* Treat the parameter as additional state with equation $
u'=0$. This extended field is holomorphic, so differentiating its real $C^1$ flow with respect to any conjugate initial coordinate gives a homogeneous complex linear variational equation with zero initial value; all conjugate-coordinate derivatives vanish by uniqueness. Hence [F6] gives holomorphy in both phase and parameter variables. Since $F$ is affine in $I$, the equation $\vartheta'=F_I(\vartheta,
u)$ is independent of $I$. With this angle trajectory fixed, $I'=-F_\vartheta(I,\vartheta_t,
u)$ is a linear inhomogeneous equation in $I$, so its solution depends affinely on the initial action. This proves the stated structure.

*Exact transformed identity.* For a fixed initial point set $G(t)=(N+\chi_t)\circ\Phi_t$, where $\chi_t=\widehat R+t(R-\widehat R)$. Using [F5] and $\{N,F\}=-(R-\widehat R)$, one obtains $G'(t)=\bigl(R-\widehat R+\{N,F\}+\{\chi_t,F\}\bigr)\circ\Phi_t=\{\chi_t,F\}\circ\Phi_t$. The endpoint values are $G(0)=N+\widehat R$ and $G(1)=(N+R)\circ\Phi$. Integrating and then adding $(P-R)\circ\Phi$ proves the exact identity in clause 3 on the full time-one domain.

*Periodicity, reality, and canonicity.* The Fourier polynomial $F$ is periodic, and consequently $X_F(I,\vartheta+2\pi k,\nu)=X_F(I,\vartheta,\nu)$. Translating a trajectory by $(0,2\pi k)$ and invoking uniqueness proves equivariance. On real points the data satisfy $R_{-k}=\overline{R_k}$ and the real frequencies give $F_{-k}=\overline{F_k}$; hence $F$ and its field are real there, and uniqueness preserves reality. By [F5] the real flow is canonical. The same symplectic identity holds on the complex domain directly: in the constant matrix representing $\omega$, the Hamiltonian Jacobian satisfies $(DX_F)^{\mathsf T}J+JDX_F=0$, by symmetry of the Hessian of $F$; differentiating $(D\Phi_t)^{\mathsf T}J(D\Phi_t)$ using step 3.1 therefore gives zero derivative and initial value $J$. This proves canonicity throughout the complex domain as well.

*Remainder on the shrinking action domain.* On $D_{\eta r,s-8\sigma,h}$ the trajectories lie in $D_{2\eta r,s-7\sigma,h}$ by step 2.1. Thus [F2] gives $|(P-R)\circ\Phi|\le C[\eta^2+\sigma^{-n}e^{-\sigma K/2}]\varepsilon$. Moreover, on every trajectory, $|R_\vartheta|\le C\sigma^{-n-1}\varepsilon$, $|R_I|\le C\sigma^{-n}\varepsilon/r$, and $|\widehat R_I|\le C\varepsilon/r$ because $[R]=[Q]$ and each action-Taylor coefficient at zero is bounded by $\varepsilon/r$ by Cauchy. Since $\widehat R_\vartheta=0$, these imply $|\chi_{t,\vartheta}|\le C\sigma^{-n-1}\varepsilon$ and $|\chi_{t,I}|\le C\sigma^{-n}\varepsilon/r$. Step 1.1 gives $|F_I|\le CE\sigma^{n+2}$ and $|F_\vartheta|\le CEr\sigma^{n+1}$. Therefore $|\{\chi_t,F\}|\le |\chi_{t,\vartheta}|_1|F_I|_\infty+|\chi_{t,I}|_1|F_\vartheta|_\infty\le CE\varepsilon\sigma\le CE\varepsilon$. Integrating this bound in the identity of step 3.3 proves clause 3.

*Mean frequency shift.* Since the cutoff preserves the zero Fourier mode, $\widehat R=[Q]$; hence $v_j=[\partial_{I_j}P(0,\cdot,
u)]$. Cauchy's estimate at the centre of $B_r$ gives $|\partial_{I_j}P(0,\vartheta,
u)|\le\varepsilon/r$ (take radii tending upward to $r$), and taking a real angular mean does not increase this bound. Thus $|v|\le C\varepsilon/r=B$ on $O_h$, without a Fourier-loss factor. The mean is holomorphic in $
u$ and real on real points. On $O_{h/2}$, coordinate Cauchy estimates with radius $h/2$ bound each entry of $Dv$ by $2B/h$; the induced maximum-norm operator bound is consequently $2nB/h$. Finally $\varepsilon/r=\alpha E\sigma^\mu$ by definition. This proves clause 4 and completes the step.

The Statement specifies this case: The time flow and variation estimates hold for every t in [0,1]. The exact Lie-transform integral uses both endpoints, and the time-one retained domain has angle width s-8 sigma.

The Statement specifies this case: The affine generator determines a unique local flow and the mean determines its frequency shift. No family of arbitrarily selected trajectories occurs; analytic suppliers are applied under their stated hypotheses.

citations.quote:
Throughout, fix an integer $n\ge1$. The space $\mathbb R^n$ is read through
[[rem-complex-euclidean-space-dictionary]] and $\mathbb C^n$ carries the polydisc
geometry of [[def-balls-and-polydiscs-in-complex-euclidean-space]]. All norms
below are supremum norms: for $z\in\mathbb C^m$,

$$|z|_\infty:=\max_{1\le i\le m}|z_i|,\qquad |z|_1:=\sum_{i=1}^m|z_i| .$$

**Angular torus.** Let $\mathbb Z$ be the integers ([[def-integers]]). Write
$k=(k_1,\dots,k_n)\in\mathbb Z^n$, $|k|_1=|k_1|+\dots+|k_n|$, and let
$(2\pi\mathbb Z)^n:=\{2\pi k:k\in\mathbb Z^n\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n$. On
$\mathbb R^n$ define the relation $\vartheta\sim\vartheta'$ by
$\vartheta-\vartheta'\in(2\pi\mathbb Z)^n$. This is an equivalence relation, and
the **angular torus** is the quotient set

$$\mathbb T^n:=(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)^n:=\mathbb R^n/\!\sim$$

with the quotient topology ([[def-quotient-topology]], [[def-product-topology]]),
and canonical projection $\pi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb T^n$, which is continuous
([[def-continuous-map-top]]). A map $f:\mathbb R^n\to X$ is **$2\pi$-periodic** if
$f(\vartheta+2\pi k)=f(\vartheta)$ for all $\vartheta\in\mathbb R^n$,
$k\in\mathbb Z^n$; such an $f$ factors uniquely through $\pi$, and a map on
$\mathbb T^n$ is, by definition, a $2\pi$-periodic map on $\mathbb R^n$ read
through this factorisation. A function on $\mathbb T^n$ is **continuous**, resp.
**real analytic**, when its $2\pi$-periodic representative has that property.

**Action-angle neighbourhoods.** For $0<r$ and $0<s\le\infty$ put

$$B_r:=\{I\in\mathbb C^n:|I|_\infty<r\},\qquad S_s:=\{\vartheta\in\mathbb C^n:|\mathrm{Im}\,\vartheta|_\infty<s\},$$

and, for a set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ (always measurably or
topologically qualified in the uses below) and $h\ge0$,

$$O_h(\Omega):=\{\nu\in\mathbb C^n:\operatorname{dist}_\infty(\nu,\Omega)<h\}, \qquad \operatorname{dist}_\infty(\nu,\Omega):=\inf_{\omega\in\Omega}|\nu-\omega|_\infty .$$

For $\Omega=\varnothing$ the infimum is taken in the extended nonnegative reals with $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$, so $O_h(\varnothing)=\varnothing$ for every finite $h\ge0$. Supremum norms of functions on an empty domain are $0$ (the supremum in $[0,+\infty]$). Thus an empty Diophantine label set gives an empty parameter family; results quantified over its labels are vacuous, and positive-measure assertions require their separately stated hypotheses.

The **action-angle neighbourhood** of width $(r,s,h)$ over $\Omega$ is the open
product

$$D_{r,s,h}(\Omega):=B_r\times S_s\times O_h(\Omega)\subseteq\mathbb C^{2n}\times\mathbb C^n,$$

and $D_{r,s}(\Omega):=B_r\times S_s$. In the KAM construction the parameter set
is a **frequency label set** $\Omega_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ (defined below)
and the relevant parameter neighbourhoods are $O_h(\Omega_\alpha)$; the
temperature of a step is measured by the three widths $r,s,h$ and an angular
margin $\sigma>0$.

**Holomorphic data and norms.** A function $g:D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$
is **holomorphic on $D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)$** when it is continuous and separately
holomorphic in each of the $2n+n$ complex variables
([[def-separately-holomorphic-function]],
[[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]); equivalently, by
[[thm-power-series-expansion-in-several-complex-variables]], it is given near
every point by an absolutely convergent power series in the $(I,\vartheta,\nu)$
variables. The **sup-norms** are

$$|g|_{r,s}:=|g|_{r,s,0}:=\sup_{D_{r,s}(\Omega)}|g|,\qquad |g|_{r,s,h}:=|g|_{r,s,h}(\Omega):=\sup_{D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)}|g|\in[0,+\infty].$$

Where no parameter occurs we write $g\in\mathcal H_{r,s}$ if $g$ is holomorphic
on $D_{r,s}(\Omega)$ for some fixed open $\Omega$ and $|g|_{r,s}<+\infty$; and
$g\in\mathcal H_{r,s,h}$ if $g$ is holomorphic on $D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)$ with
$|g|_{r,s,h}<+\infty$. Functions of $\vartheta$ alone are read through the
$2\pi$-periodicity of the $\vartheta$-variables, so that all integrals and
norms below are well defined on $\mathbb T^n$.

**Fourier coefficients, mean and cutoff.** Let $g\in\mathcal H_{r,s}$. For
$k\in\mathbb Z^n$ and $I\in B_r$ the **Fourier coefficient** is the iterated
Riemann integral

$$g_k(I):=\frac1{(2\pi)^n}\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\cdots\!\int_0^{2\pi} g(I,\vartheta)\,e^{-ik\cdot\vartheta}\,d\vartheta_n\cdots d\vartheta_1 ,$$

as in [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]]; by
[[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]] it equals the multiple Riemann
integral over $[0,2\pi]^n$ and is independent of the order of integration. The
**angular mean** of $g$ is $[g]:=g_0$, so $[g](I)=\frac1{(2\pi)^n}\int_{[0,2\pi]^n}g(I,\vartheta)\,d\vartheta$;
$g$ is **zero-mean** if $[g]=0$ for every $I\in B_r$. For a real number $K\ge0$
the **Fourier cutoff** $T_Kg$ is the trigonometric polynomial

$$T_Kg(I,\vartheta):=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n,\ |k|_1\le K}g_k(I)\,e^{ik\cdot\vartheta}.$$

The sum is finite because $|k|_1\le K$ bounds each $|k_i|$ by $K$. For a
function $g$ of $(I,\vartheta,\nu)$ the same notations apply with the
$\nu$-variable carried along; e.g. $[g]$, $g_k$ and $T_Kg$ are then functions of
$(I,\nu)$.

**Frequency label sets.** Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $\alpha>0$
and $\tau>n-1$. A frequency $\nu\in\mathbb R^n$ is **$(\alpha,\tau)$-Diophantine**
if

$$|k\cdot\nu|\ge\alpha\,|k|_1^{-\tau}\qquad\text{for every }k\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\},$$

with $k\cdot\nu=\sum_ik_i\nu_i$. The **label set** is

$$\Omega_{\alpha,\tau}:=\Omega\cap\{\nu\in\mathbb R^n:\nu\text{ is }(\alpha,\tau)\text{-Diophantine}\}.$$

$\Omega_{\alpha,\tau}$ is closed in $\Omega$ and contained in the global
$(\alpha,\tau)$-Diophantine set; it need not have interior points. Write
$\widehat\Omega:=\Omega$ when $\tau,\alpha$ are fixed and no confusion arises.
The parameter neighbourhoods used below are $O_h(\Omega_{\alpha,\tau})$.

**Hamiltonians, canonical form and Poisson bracket.** A **Hamiltonian datum**
on $D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)$ is a holomorphic $H:D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$ which
is real-valued on real points; more generally we consider families
$H(I,\vartheta;\nu)=e(\nu)+\nu\cdot I+P(I,\vartheta,\nu)$ where $e$ is
holomorphic on $O_h(\Omega)$ and real on real points, and
$P\in\mathcal H_{r,s,h}$ is real on real points. Pair the coordinates as
$q=\vartheta$, $p=I$ in the phase-domain notation of
[[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]; the **standard
two-form** in these coordinates is

$$\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n d\vartheta_i\wedge dI_i,$$

and the **Hamiltonian vector field** of a $C^1$ Hamiltonian $H$ is, by
[[prop-cm-hamiltonian-field-and-poisson-bracket-in-a-phase-chart]] with
$(q,p)=(\vartheta,I)$,

$$X_H=(H_I,-H_\vartheta),\qquad \theta'=H_I,\quad I'=-H_\vartheta\ \ \text{(Hamilton's equations)},$$

characterised by $\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$; the **Poisson bracket** is

$$\{f,g\}=f_\vartheta\cdot g_I-f_I\cdot g_\vartheta,\qquad \{f,g\}=\nabla f^{\mathsf T}J\nabla g\ \ \text{in the notation of that item}.$$

In particular $\{f,e+\nu\cdot I\}=\nu\cdot f_\vartheta$ for every
$C^1$ function $f$.

**Angular parametrisations and Lagrangian images.** Fix a Hamiltonian datum
$H$. An **angular parametrisation** is a map $\psi=(\psi_I,\psi_\vartheta)$
with $\psi_I:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb C^n$ $2\pi$-periodic and
$\psi_\vartheta:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb C^n$ satisfying
$\psi_\vartheta(\vartheta+2\pi k)=\psi_\vartheta(\vartheta)+2\pi k$ for all
$k\in\mathbb Z^n$, so that
$\pi\circ\psi_\vartheta=\pi\circ(\psi_\vartheta\big|_{\mathbb R^n})$ descends to
$\mathbb T^n$; it is **holomorphic on the strip $S_s$** when both components
extend holomorphically to $S_s$, and **real analytic** when in addition
$\psi(\mathbb R^n)\subseteq\mathbb R^{2n}$ and the components are real analytic
in the real variables. It is **faithful** if
$\psi(\vartheta)=\psi(\vartheta')$ implies
$\vartheta-\vartheta'\in(2\pi\mathbb Z)^n$, and an **immersion** if
$D\psi(\vartheta)$ has rank $n$ for every $\vartheta\in\mathbb R^n$; a tuple
that is both is an **embedded torus parametrisation**. Its image is
**Lagrangian** (with respect to $\omega$) if
$\psi^*\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n d(\psi_\vartheta)_i\wedge d(\psi_I)_i=0$ as a
two-form on the parameter space of the representative, and **invariant with
frequency $\nu$** if

$$X_H(\psi(\vartheta))=\sum_{j=1}^n\nu_j\,\partial_{\vartheta_j}\psi(\vartheta) \qquad\text{for all real }\vartheta .$$

Throughout, fix an integer $n\ge1$. The space $\mathbb R^n$ is read through
[[rem-complex-euclidean-space-dictionary]] and $\mathbb C^n$ carries the polydisc
geometry of [[def-balls-and-polydiscs-in-complex-euclidean-space]]. All norms
below are supremum norms: for $z\in\mathbb C^m$,

$$|z|_\infty:=\max_{1\le i\le m}|z_i|,\qquad |z|_1:=\sum_{i=1}^m|z_i| .$$

**Angular torus.** Let $\mathbb Z$ be the integers ([[def-integers]]). Write
$k=(k_1,\dots,k_n)\in\mathbb Z^n$, $|k|_1=|k_1|+\dots+|k_n|$, and let
$(2\pi\mathbb Z)^n:=\{2\pi k:k\in\mathbb Z^n\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n$. On
$\mathbb R^n$ define the relation $\vartheta\sim\vartheta'$ by
$\vartheta-\vartheta'\in(2\pi\mathbb Z)^n$. This is an equivalence relation, and
the **angular torus** is the quotient set

$$\mathbb T^n:=(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)^n:=\mathbb R^n/\!\sim$$

with the quotient topology ([[def-quotient-topology]], [[def-product-topology]]),
and canonical projection $\pi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb T^n$, which is continuous
([[def-continuous-map-top]]). A map $f:\mathbb R^n\to X$ is **$2\pi$-periodic** if
$f(\vartheta+2\pi k)=f(\vartheta)$ for all $\vartheta\in\mathbb R^n$,
$k\in\mathbb Z^n$; such an $f$ factors uniquely through $\pi$, and a map on
$\mathbb T^n$ is, by definition, a $2\pi$-periodic map on $\mathbb R^n$ read
through this factorisation. A function on $\mathbb T^n$ is **continuous**, resp.
**real analytic**, when its $2\pi$-periodic representative has that property.

**Action-angle neighbourhoods.** For $0<r$ and $0<s\le\infty$ put

$$B_r:=\{I\in\mathbb C^n:|I|_\infty<r\},\qquad S_s:=\{\vartheta\in\mathbb C^n:|\mathrm{Im}\,\vartheta|_\infty<s\},$$

and, for a set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ (always measurably or
topologically qualified in the uses below) and $h\ge0$,

$$O_h(\Omega):=\{\nu\in\mathbb C^n:\operatorname{dist}_\infty(\nu,\Omega)<h\}, \qquad \operatorname{dist}_\infty(\nu,\Omega):=\inf_{\omega\in\Omega}|\nu-\omega|_\infty .$$

For $\Omega=\varnothing$ the infimum is taken in the extended nonnegative reals with $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$, so $O_h(\varnothing)=\varnothing$ for every finite $h\ge0$. Supremum norms of functions on an empty domain are $0$ (the supremum in $[0,+\infty]$). Thus an empty Diophantine label set gives an empty parameter family; results quantified over its labels are vacuous, and positive-measure assertions require their separately stated hypotheses.

The **action-angle neighbourhood** of width $(r,s,h)$ over $\Omega$ is the open
product

$$D_{r,s,h}(\Omega):=B_r\times S_s\times O_h(\Omega)\subseteq\mathbb C^{2n}\times\mathbb C^n,$$

and $D_{r,s}(\Omega):=B_r\times S_s$. In the KAM construction the parameter set
is a **frequency label set** $\Omega_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ (defined below)
and the relevant parameter neighbourhoods are $O_h(\Omega_\alpha)$; the
temperature of a step is measured by the three widths $r,s,h$ and an angular
margin $\sigma>0$.

**Holomorphic data and norms.** A function $g:D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$
is **holomorphic on $D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)$** when it is continuous and separately
holomorphic in each of the $2n+n$ complex variables
([[def-separately-holomorphic-function]],
[[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]); equivalently, by
[[thm-power-series-expansion-in-several-complex-variables]], it is given near
every point by an absolutely convergent power series in the $(I,\vartheta,\nu)$
variables. The **sup-norms** are

$$|g|_{r,s}:=|g|_{r,s,0}:=\sup_{D_{r,s}(\Omega)}|g|,\qquad |g|_{r,s,h}:=|g|_{r,s,h}(\Omega):=\sup_{D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)}|g|\in[0,+\infty].$$

Where no parameter occurs we write $g\in\mathcal H_{r,s}$ if $g$ is holomorphic
on $D_{r,s}(\Omega)$ for some fixed open $\Omega$ and $|g|_{r,s}<+\infty$; and
$g\in\mathcal H_{r,s,h}$ if $g$ is holomorphic on $D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)$ with
$|g|_{r,s,h}<+\infty$. Functions of $\vartheta$ alone are read through the
$2\pi$-periodicity of the $\vartheta$-variables, so that all integrals and
norms below are well defined on $\mathbb T^n$.

**Fourier coefficients, mean and cutoff.** Let $g\in\mathcal H_{r,s}$. For
$k\in\mathbb Z^n$ and $I\in B_r$ the **Fourier coefficient** is the iterated
Riemann integral

$$g_k(I):=\frac1{(2\pi)^n}\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\cdots\!\int_0^{2\pi} g(I,\vartheta)\,e^{-ik\cdot\vartheta}\,d\vartheta_n\cdots d\vartheta_1 ,$$

as in [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]]; by
[[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]] it equals the multiple Riemann
integral over $[0,2\pi]^n$ and is independent of the order of integration. The
**angular mean** of $g$ is $[g]:=g_0$, so $[g](I)=\frac1{(2\pi)^n}\int_{[0,2\pi]^n}g(I,\vartheta)\,d\vartheta$;
$g$ is **zero-mean** if $[g]=0$ for every $I\in B_r$. For a real number $K\ge0$
the **Fourier cutoff** $T_Kg$ is the trigonometric polynomial

$$T_Kg(I,\vartheta):=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n,\ |k|_1\le K}g_k(I)\,e^{ik\cdot\vartheta}.$$

The sum is finite because $|k|_1\le K$ bounds each $|k_i|$ by $K$. For a
function $g$ of $(I,\vartheta,\nu)$ the same notations apply with the
$\nu$-variable carried along; e.g. $[g]$, $g_k$ and $T_Kg$ are then functions of
$(I,\nu)$.

**Frequency label sets.** Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $\alpha>0$
and $\tau>n-1$. A frequency $\nu\in\mathbb R^n$ is **$(\alpha,\tau)$-Diophantine**
if

$$|k\cdot\nu|\ge\alpha\,|k|_1^{-\tau}\qquad\text{for every }k\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\},$$

with $k\cdot\nu=\sum_ik_i\nu_i$. The **label set** is

$$\Omega_{\alpha,\tau}:=\Omega\cap\{\nu\in\mathbb R^n:\nu\text{ is }(\alpha,\tau)\text{-Diophantine}\}.$$

$\Omega_{\alpha,\tau}$ is closed in $\Omega$ and contained in the global
$(\alpha,\tau)$-Diophantine set; it need not have interior points. Write
$\widehat\Omega:=\Omega$ when $\tau,\alpha$ are fixed and no confusion arises.
The parameter neighbourhoods used below are $O_h(\Omega_{\alpha,\tau})$.

**Hamiltonians, canonical form and Poisson bracket.** A **Hamiltonian datum**
on $D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)$ is a holomorphic $H:D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$ which
is real-valued on real points; more generally we consider families
$H(I,\vartheta;\nu)=e(\nu)+\nu\cdot I+P(I,\vartheta,\nu)$ where $e$ is
holomorphic on $O_h(\Omega)$ and real on real points, and
$P\in\mathcal H_{r,s,h}$ is real on real points. Pair the coordinates as
$q=\vartheta$, $p=I$ in the phase-domain notation of
[[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]; the **standard
two-form** in these coordinates is

$$\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n d\vartheta_i\wedge dI_i,$$

and the **Hamiltonian vector field** of a $C^1$ Hamiltonian $H$ is, by
[[prop-cm-hamiltonian-field-and-poisson-bracket-in-a-phase-chart]] with
$(q,p)=(\vartheta,I)$,

$$X_H=(H_I,-H_\vartheta),\qquad \theta'=H_I,\quad I'=-H_\vartheta\ \ \text{(Hamilton's equations)},$$

characterised by $\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$; the **Poisson bracket** is

$$\{f,g\}=f_\vartheta\cdot g_I-f_I\cdot g_\vartheta,\qquad \{f,g\}=\nabla f^{\mathsf T}J\nabla g\ \ \text{in the notation of that item}.$$

In particular $\{f,e+\nu\cdot I\}=\nu\cdot f_\vartheta$ for every
$C^1$ function $f$.

**Angular parametrisations and Lagrangian images.** Fix a Hamiltonian datum
$H$. An **angular parametrisation** is a map $\psi=(\psi_I,\psi_\vartheta)$
with $\psi_I:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb C^n$ $2\pi$-periodic and
$\psi_\vartheta:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb C^n$ satisfying
$\psi_\vartheta(\vartheta+2\pi k)=\psi_\vartheta(\vartheta)+2\pi k$ for all
$k\in\mathbb Z^n$, so that
$\pi\circ\psi_\vartheta=\pi\circ(\psi_\vartheta\big|_{\mathbb R^n})$ descends to
$\mathbb T^n$; it is **holomorphic on the strip $S_s$** when both components
extend holomorphically to $S_s$, and **real analytic** when in addition
$\psi(\mathbb R^n)\subseteq\mathbb R^{2n}$ and the components are real analytic
in the real variables. It is **faithful** if
$\psi(\vartheta)=\psi(\vartheta')$ implies
$\vartheta-\vartheta'\in(2\pi\mathbb Z)^n$, and an **immersion** if
$D\psi(\vartheta)$ has rank $n$ for every $\vartheta\in\mathbb R^n$; a tuple
that is both is an **embedded torus parametrisation**. Its image is
**Lagrangian** (with respect to $\omega$) if
$\psi^*\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n d(\psi_\vartheta)_i\wedge d(\psi_I)_i=0$ as a
two-form on the parameter space of the representative, and **invariant with
frequency $\nu$** if

$$X_H(\psi(\vartheta))=\sum_{j=1}^n\nu_j\,\partial_{\vartheta_j}\psi(\vartheta) \qquad\text{for all real }\vartheta .$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ and every real $a>0$,
$$\frac{x^m}{\exp(ax)}\longrightarrow0\qquad(x\to+\infty).$$

derivations.claim: Since $C_*\sqrt{E_0}\le q<1$, induction gives $E_{j+1}/E_j=C_*\sqrt{E_j}\le q$ and $E_j\le q^jE_0$. Thus $\sqrt{E_j}\le c$, $\eta_j\le1/8$, and $\eta_j/\sigma_j\le(\sqrt{E_0}/\sigma_0)(2\sqrt q)^j\le1$. This proves (b) and the assertions about $\eta_j$ in (a). Also induction directly gives $E_j=A^{(3/2)^j}/C_*^2$, so $\log E_j=-(3/2)^j|\log A|-2\log C_*$ because $0<A\le q^2<1$.

The action radii decrease because $\eta_j\le1/8$, and $\sigma_j\le\sigma_0\le1$. Further, $K_j\sigma_j=K_0\sigma_02^j\ge1$ and $h_j\le h_0\le1$. By the geometric series, $\sum_{i<j}\sigma_i=2\sigma_0(1-2^{-j})$, whence $s_j=s_0-16\sigma_0+16\sigma_j$ and $s_j-8\sigma_j=s_0-16\sigma_0+8\sigma_j\ge s_0/2$. Since $\sigma_j\le\sigma_0\le s_0/32\le s_j/8$, all remaining assertions of (a) follow.

The inequality $E_j\le c\eta_j$ gives the first bound in (c). For the other bound, divide by $h_jr_j$: $\varepsilon_j/(h_jr_j)=\alpha E_j\sigma_0^\mu4^{\mu j}2^{-\mu j}/h_0\le(\alpha E_0\sigma_0^\mu/h_0)2^{-(\mu+2)j}\le1/D\le c$, using $E_j\le4^{-(\mu+1)j}E_0$ and condition 3. Thus (c) holds at every step.

Since $\mu>\tau+1$, condition 3 yields $h_j\le[\alpha/(2K_0^{\tau+1})]4^{-\mu j}\le\alpha/(2K_0^{\tau+1}4^{(\tau+1)j})=\alpha/(2K_j^{\tau+1})$, and $h_{j+1}/h_j=4^{-\mu}\le1/4$. Moreover $E_j/h_{j+1}\le4^\mu(E_0/h_0)4^{-j}$, and hence $B_j/h_{j+1}\le(C4^\mu\alpha E_0\sigma_0^\mu/h_0)2^{-(\mu+2)j}\le1/(16n)$ by $D\ge16nC4^\mu$. This proves (d) and (f). In particular [F2] applies on $O_{h_{j+1}}\subseteq O_{h_j/4}$, and its image lies in $O_{h_j/2}$.

Put $a:=|\log A|$ and $b:=n\log(1/\sigma_0)+2\log C_*$. All these quantities are nonnegative. Condition 2 and [F3] give $K_j\sigma_j/2\ge L\,2^j\ge a(3/2)^j+b+nj\log2+1$, using separately $2^j\ge(3/2)^j$, $2^j\ge1$ and $2^j\ge j$. Therefore $\log(\sigma_j^{-n}e^{-K_j\sigma_j/2})\le n\log(1/\sigma_0)+nj\log2-a(3/2)^j-b-nj\log2-1=\log E_j-1$. Exponentiation proves (e).

Since $r_j+\sigma_j\le r_0+\sigma_0$, the first sum in (g) is at most $(r_0+\sigma_0)E_0\sum_j4^{-j}\le4(r_0+\sigma_0)E_0$. Also $\sum_jE_j\le(4/3)E_0\le2E_0$ and $\sum_j2^jE_j\le E_0\sum_j2^{-j}=2E_0$. Step 2.2 gives $\sum_j\varepsilon_j/(r_jh_j)\le(\alpha E_0\sigma_0^\mu/h_0)\sum_j2^{-(\mu+2)j}\le(4/3)\alpha E_0\sigma_0^\mu/h_0$. These establish (g) without any assumption relating $r_0$ to $\sigma_0$.

The definitions give $\varepsilon_{j+1}/\varepsilon_j=(E_{j+1}/E_j)(r_{j+1}/r_j)(\sigma_{j+1}/\sigma_j)^\mu=C_*\sqrt{E_j}\sqrt{E_j}2^{-\mu}=C_*2^{-\mu}E_j\ge3CE_j$. By (e) and $\eta_j^2=E_j$, the remainder bound of [F1] is at most $3CE_j\varepsilon_j\le\varepsilon_{j+1}$. Retraction only evaluates this holomorphic remainder on its parameter subdomain by step 2.3 and [F2], so it cannot increase its sup-norm. The retained widths are $r_{j+1}=\eta_jr_j$ and $s_{j+1}=s_j-8\sigma_j$.

To check feasibility, choose $K_0=\lceil\max(1,2L)/\sigma_0\rceil$ and $h_0=\min(1,\alpha/(2K_0^{\tau+1}))$. As $E_0\downarrow0$, this cutoff is bounded by a constant times $1+|\log E_0|$, so $2DE_0\sigma_0^\mu K_0^{\tau+1}\to0$. For completeness, with $t=|\log E_0|$, choose an integer $m>\tau+1$; for $t\ge1$, $(1+t)^{\tau+1}\le2^{\tau+1}t^m$, so [F4] implies $e^{-t}(1+t)^{\tau+1}\to0$. Thus for all sufficiently small $E_0$ one has $D E_0\sigma_0^\mu\le1/(2K_0^{\tau+1})$, and, for each fixed $\alpha$, also $D\alpha E_0\sigma_0^\mu\le1$. These are exactly the two inequalities needed for condition 3 with the chosen $h_0$. If $\alpha\le1$, the second follows already from the first since $K_0\ge1$; all thresholds are then independent of $\alpha$. Conditions 1 and 2 hold by further decreasing $E_0$ and by the cutoff choice. This proves simultaneous feasibility and completes the lemma.

boundaries.evidence: The sums in clause (g) include the empty initial sum with value 0 and are stated for all j>=0; step 3.1 evaluates them from the geometric bounds and no empty family is discarded.
The case j=0 (the initial stage) is included in every clause; step 1.1 provides the base of the induction and the displayed sum bounds start at j=0.
The statement holds for every n>=2 and the estimates use n only through explicit constants; nothing in steps 1.1-3.1 is specific to a choice of dimension beyond the hypotheses.

Initial conditions 1-3 permit equality at their listed smallness and cutoff bounds. Proof 2.2-2.4 checks the weak parameter, shift and tail inequalities, including B_j<=h_{j+1}/(16n), rather than the former slower parameter schedule.
At j=0 all initial conditions are used directly. Proof 2.1 gives s_j-8 sigma_j>=s_0/2, and Proof 4.1 chooses the upper endpoint h_0=min(1,alpha/(2K_0^{tau+1})) after verifying its lower endpoint.
The recurrence, cutoff ceiling and frequency width in Proof 4.1 are explicit. Geometric sums and the exponential-dominance supplier verify feasibility without simultaneous arbitrary selections.
